title: Spring (device)
description: Elastic object that stores mechanical energy
wiki_lead:
A spring is a device consisting of an elastic but largely rigid material (typically metal) bent or molded into a form (especially a coil) that can return into shape after being compressed, extended or twisted. Springs can store energy when compressed, when extended, and/or when twisted. In everyday use, the term most often refers to coil springs, but there are many different spring designs. Modern springs are typically manufactured from spring steel. An example of a non-metallic spring is the bow, made traditionally of flexible  yew wood, which when drawn stores energy to propel an arrow.
When a conventional spring, without stiffness variability features, is compressed or stretched from its resting position, it exerts an opposing force approximately proportional to its change in length (this approximation breaks down for larger deflections). The rate or spring constant of a spring is the change in the force it exerts, divided by the change in deflection of the spring. That is, it is the gradient of the force versus deflection curve. An extension or compression spring's rate is expressed in units of force divided by distance, for example or N/m or lbf/in. A torsion spring is a spring that works by twisting; when it is twisted about its axis by an angle, it produces a torque proportional to the angle. A torsion spring's rate is in units of torque divided by angle, such as N·m/rad or ft·lbf/degree. The inverse of spring rate is compliance, that is: if a spring has a rate of 10 N/mm, it has a compliance of 0.1 mm/N. The stiffness (or rate) of springs in parallel is additive, as is the compliance of springs in series.
Springs are made from a variety of elastic materials, the most common being spring steel. Small springs can be wound from pre-hardened stock, while larger ones are made from annealed steel and hardened after manufacture. Some non-ferrous metals are also used, including phosphor bronze and titanium for parts requiring corrosion resistance, and low-resistance beryllium copper for springs carrying electric current.

Some non-ferrous metals are also used, including phosphor bronze and titanium for parts requiring corrosion resistance, and low-resistance beryllium copper for springs carrying electric current.


History
Simple non-coiled springs have been used throughout human history, e.g. the bow (and arrow). In the Bronze Age more sophisticated spring devices were used, as shown by the spread of tweezers in many cultures. Ctesibius of Alexandria developed a method for making springs out of an alloy of bronze with an increased proportion of tin, hardened by hammering after it was cast.
Coiled springs appeared early in the 15th century, in door locks. The first spring-powered clocks appeared in that century and evolved into the first large watches by the 16th century.
In 1676 British physicist Robert Hooke postulated Hooke's law, which states that the force a spring exerts is proportional to its extension.
On March 8, 1850, John Evans, Founder of John Evans' Sons, Incorporated, opened his business in New Haven, Connecticut, manufacturing flat springs for carriages and other vehicles, as well as the machinery to manufacture the springs. Evans was a Welsh blacksmith and springmaker who emigrated to the United States in 1847, John Evans' Sons became "America's oldest springmaker" and continues to operate today.


Types


Classification

Springs can be classified depending on how the load force is applied to them.

Tension/extension spring
The spring is designed to operate with a tension load, so the spring stretches as the load is applied to it.
Compression spring
Designed to operate with a compression load, so the spring gets shorter as the load is applied to it.
Torsion spring
Unlike the above types in which the load is an axial force, the load applied to a torsion spring is a torque or twisting force, and the end of the spring rotates through an angle as the load is applied. Often used in torsion bar vehicle suspension systems.
There are many other ways to potentially classify and subclassify springs, such as their shape - coil springs are common, but so are leaf springs, for example.  Garter springs are arc spring
grok_lead: A spring is a mechanical device that stores potential energy through elastic deformation under an applied force or torque and releases that energy upon relaxation, returning to its original configuration. Typically fabricated from resilient materials such as high-carbon steel, brass, or other alloys capable of undergoing significant elastic strain without permanent damage, springs function as compliant elements in mechanical systems to exert controlled forces. Their performance adheres to Hooke's law, which describes the restorative force $ F $ as directly proportional to the displacement $ x $ from equilibrium, expressed as $ F = -kx $, where $ k $ is the spring constant representing stiffness. Springs are classified into several primary types based on their geometry and loading mode, each suited to specific engineering needs. Helical compression springs, coiled from round wire, absorb energy by shortening under axial load and are common in automotive suspensions and machinery buffers. Extension springs, also helical but with hooks at ends, elongate under tension to provide pulling forces, as seen in trampolines and garage doors. Torsion springs resist rotational forces through twisting, powering devices like clothespins and clock mechanisms. Flat or leaf springs, made from stacked strips, handle bending loads in vehicle axles and bows. Additionally, disc or Belleville springs deliver high loads in compact forms for applications like bolted joints and valves. Materials selection emphasizes high yield strength and fatigue resistance, with wire diameters and coil indices optimized to minimize stress concentrations during operation. The utility of springs spans diverse fields, from everyday consumer products to advanced engineering systems, enabling functions like shock absorption, motion control, and energy storage. In vehicles, leaf and coil springs maintain ride comfort by damping vibrations; in precision instruments, constant-force springs ensure uniform tension in retractable devices like tape measures. Industrial applications include valve timing in engines and safety mechanisms in elevators, where springs must withstand cyclic loading without failure. Design considerations, such as buckling prevention and fatigue life under repeated deflection, are critical, often analyzed using factors of safety based on material properties and load conditions. Springs have a long history dating back to prehistoric times, with early uses in bows and traps, evolving through ancient metal forms and medieval mechanisms to modern applications in nanomaterials and composites for microscale uses in electronics and biomedicine.
